name: Cherbourg
title: Cherbourg Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging | Ferries & Cargo Ships
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Cherbourg for ferries to Poole, Portsmouth and Ireland, cargo ships and offshore vessels: decks, ballast tanks and piping.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Ships in the Cherbourg Roadstead and Harbour
intro: Cherbourg sits at the tip of the Cotentin peninsula, behind one of the largest artificial roadsteads in the world, and it handles ferries for England and Ireland, cargo ships, cruise calls and the vessels of the offshore energy industry. That mix gives a steady flow of ships stopped in sheltered water. Atlantis mobilises technicians from India to measure hulls, decks and tanks at the quay or in the roadstead as each schedule allows.

highlights.p: The breakwater roadstead gives ships a protected anchorage off the Cotentin. A ship waiting for a berth or orders can be gauged at anchor by launch when the sea state allows, with deck and ballast tank readings first.
The passenger terminal handles ro-pax ships on Channel and Irish Sea routes. Layovers in port give windows for vehicle deck, ramp and tank readings between sailings, as the schedule permits.
Component cargoes for offshore wind, project cargo and bulk calls bring heavy-lift and multipurpose ships to the quays. Longer stays on those berths suit holds, decks and hatch cover gauging.

port.h: Cherbourg: a naval harbour with a civilian side
p: Cherbourg lies on the northern coast of the Cotentin, facing the English Channel, and its harbour is shaped by a long breakwater that encloses a large roadstead. Behind it are two worlds: the French Navy's arsenal, which builds and supports submarines and is closed to civilians, and the commercial port, which is run by the regional authority Ports de Normandie. The commercial harbour has a passenger terminal, ro-ro and general cargo quays and berths for bulk, project and offshore cargoes. The roadstead is wide enough to hold a number of ships at anchor, and its shelter makes it a convenient place to wait for orders or weather.

Ferries are the best-known traffic. Services leave Cherbourg for ports in southern England and for Ireland, using ro-pax ships that carry passengers, cars and freight lorries, and the terminal sees ships at all hours. Cruise ships anchor in the roadstead or berth at the quay on summer calls. Cargo traffic is varied: bulk and general cargo, timber, agricultural products, and project loads such as wind turbine components moving to and from the offshore industry. Ships serving offshore wind farms in the Channel use the harbour as a base for supplies and crew, which adds service vessels and support ships to the mix.

For thickness gauging, Cherbourg gives three kinds of window. Ferries lie alongside between sailings, sometimes for a few hours, sometimes for a night. Cargo and project ships may stay on the quay for days while loading or waiting for weather in the Channel. Ships at anchor in the roadstead have time but need a launch. The port has repair and maintenance facilities for small and mid-sized ships, but the large ships that stop here normally dock at a bigger yard elsewhere, so readings taken during a Cherbourg stay are used as a steel estimate for that later docking.

facilities.h: Where gauging can be done at Cherbourg
p: At the ferry terminal, thickness work follows the sailing timetable. Vehicle decks are measured when they are clear, ramp and door structure is checked while the ship is alongside, and tanks and machinery spaces are worked within the ship's permit system. Because a ferry is a passenger vessel, the superintendent and the master decide which spaces are available and which stay closed until the passengers have left. A longer layover, for instance when the ship is held by weather or schedule, opens up the larger scopes that a quick turnaround cannot.

On the cargo and project quays the pace is calmer. A multipurpose or heavy-lift ship waiting for its cargo can have its holds, hatch covers, tank top and ballast tanks gauged over a day or more, and service vessels for offshore wind give similar windows between rotations. In the roadstead, a launch booked by the ship's agent takes the team to a ship at anchor. Work there depends on swell and wind, and the priority list puts the most important spaces first, in case a change in weather ends the visit early.
list: Passenger terminal berths — vehicle deck, ramp, door and ballast tank gauging on ro-pax ferries during layovers.
Commercial quays — hold, hatch cover and tank top gauging on cargo ships during loading or while they wait for weather.
Project cargo and heavy-lift berths — deck, hatch and ballast tank readings on multipurpose ships serving the offshore wind industry.
Cherbourg roadstead anchorage — launch-served gauging on ships waiting for orders or a berth, when sea state allows.
Port repair quays — wall-thickness checks on piping and deck structure of small and mid-sized ships during repair afloat.
Offshore service vessel berths — hull and deck gauging on crew transfer and supply vessels between rotations.

context.h: Regulation and the Channel traffic picture
p: Port state control at Cherbourg belongs to the Paris MoU regime, with inspections carried out by the Centres de sécurité des navires of the French maritime administration. Ferries, cargo ships and tankers calling from British and Irish ports are all subject to risk-based targeting, so a ship with visible wastage on a vehicle deck or a corroded hatch cover is a candidate for detailed inspection. Measured thickness figures let the master show the inspector what the structure actually is, instead of arguing from appearance.

Cherbourg stands in some of the busiest water in Europe, close to the Channel traffic separation schemes, and ships that call here do so in the middle of a route that shapes their survey planning. Ferries operate on rolling refit programmes, and cargo ships are docked wherever a yard slot is available. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation's Inventory of Hazardous Materials applies to ships calling at EU ports, and EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime affect every voyage. For ESP ships such as tankers and bulk carriers the Enhanced Survey Programme sets the extent of gauging, which grows with age.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Cherbourg
jobs.p: Requests from Cherbourg reflect its variety. Ferry operators ask for deck and tank readings between sailings, owners of multipurpose ships ask for hold and hatch cover gauging on the quay, and superintendents with ships waiting in the roadstead want a first set of readings before the next yard slot. We agree the priority list with the superintendent in advance. Typical jobs include:
list: Vehicle deck, ramp and bow visor structure gauging on a ro-pax ferry during an extended layover at the passenger terminal.
Ballast tank and double-bottom readings on a cargo ship waiting at the quay for its cargo, giving a measured steel list for the next docking.
Hold, coaming and hatch cover gauging on a multipurpose ship carrying components for offshore wind.
Deck and hull gauging on an offshore service vessel between rotations, ahead of its planned refit.
Launch-served ballast tank and deck gauging on a bulk carrier waiting at anchor in the roadstead for orders.

logistics: From India the team typically flies to Paris and travels on by train through Normandy to Cherbourg, a long but straightforward journey, with the small airport near the town offering limited connections. The ship's agent arranges port passes for the terminal and quay concerned and books the launch for any work in the roadstead. The naval arsenal is closed to civilians and plays no part. Each technician needs a Schengen visa, applied for as soon as the call is confirmed, with an invitation from the owner or agent naming the ship and the port.
vessels: Ro-pax ferries to England and Ireland

faqs.q: Can a ship be gauged at anchor in the Cherbourg roadstead?
faqs.a: Yes, by launch, when swell and wind allow safe boarding. The roadstead is sheltered by its breakwater, but a change in the weather can still stop the work, so the most important spaces are measured first and the remainder is added if conditions hold. The ship's agent books the launch and confirms the boarding time.

faqs.q: How is gauging fitted around a ferry's sailing time?
faqs.a: We agree a priority list with the superintendent in advance: sections of the vehicle deck once they are clear, ramps and doors, and tanks and machinery spaces that do not depend on loading. A short turnaround gets the top of that list. A longer layover, such as an overnight stay, lets us go further down it.

faqs.q: Does Cherbourg have a drydock for a docking survey?
faqs.a: The port has repair facilities for small and mid-sized vessels, but larger ships normally dock at a bigger yard elsewhere. Gauging at Cherbourg beforehand gives that yard a measured steel list, which makes the docking shorter and its scope firmer.

faqs.q: Can offshore wind support vessels be gauged between rotations?
faqs.a: Yes. Service and crew transfer vessels lie alongside for short periods between trips, long enough for targeted hull, deck and piping readings. We coordinate with the operator's schedule so the work fits the rotation, and unfinished areas are listed for the next planned stay.
